faculty.title: Mechanical & Aerospace Engineering / Andlinger Center for Energy & the Environment
faculty.sub_field: Quantum mechanical simulation for sustainable energy
faculty.summary: Carter develops and applies quantum mechanical simulation techniques to discover and design molecules and materials for sustainable energy.

faculty.name: Bernard Chazelle
faculty.title: Computer Science
faculty.summary: His research interests include natural algorithms, multiagent dynamics, iterated learning, and evolutionary complexity.

faculty.name: David P. Dobkin
faculty.title: Professor Emeritus, Computer Science
faculty.sub_field: Computer graphics, computational geometry, and analysis of algorithms
faculty.summary: Professor Dobkin's work encompasses computer graphics, analysis of algorithms, and computational geometry, including creating high-quality images of mathematical objects, algorithms and models for image synthesis, mathematical approaches to computational issues, and computer vision and face recognition.

faculty.name: Jianqing Fan
faculty.title: Operations Research & Financial Engineering
faculty.summary: His research interests include high-dimensional statistics, machine learning, financial econometrics and risk management, bioinformatics and biostatistics, graphical and network modeling, and nonparametric and semiparametric modeling.

faculty.name: Jason Fleischer
faculty.title: Electrical and Computer Engineering
faculty.summary: Fleischer studies nonlinear optics within the broader context of general wave physics, focusing on propagation problems that are universal to wave systems. He uses optical systems for their ability to allow easy control of the input and direct imaging of the output.

faculty.name: Marc Gilles
faculty.title: Mathematics
faculty.summary: Gilles works in applied mathematics, particularly problems involving numerical linear algebra and algorithms for cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM). He developed RECOVAR, a software tool for reconstructing flexible proteins from large and noisy cryo-EM datasets.

faculty.name: Mikko P. Haataja
faculty.title: Mechanical & Aerospace Engineering
faculty.sub_field: Theoretical and computational materials science and biophysics
faculty.summary: Haataja works on evolving microstructures from materials to biology, spanning microstructure formation during solid-solid phase transformations, solidification, dislocation dynamics, and recrystallization kinetics. His work also covers biological processes including cellular signaling pathways and thermodynamics of spatial heterogeneities such as lipid rafts in cell membranes.

faculty.name: Gregory W. Hammett
faculty.title: Plasma Physics
faculty.summary: Hammett works on theory and computer simulations of plasma turbulence in fusion and astrophysical plasmas, and on advanced computational algorithms.

faculty.name: Boris Hanin
faculty.title: Operations Research & Financial Engineering
faculty.summary: Hanin's machine learning interests center on the theory of neural networks, including approximation power, statistical physics of initialization, guarantees for optimization, and generalization. His probability interests include mathematical physics, random matrix theory, Gaussian processes arising in spectral theory/quantum mechanics, and random polynomials.

faculty.name: Elad Hazan
faculty.title: Computer Science
faculty.summary: Hazan's listed research interests are machine learning and robotics.

faculty.name: Sergiu Klainerman
faculty.title: Mathematics
faculty.summary: Klainerman studies nonlinear hyperbolic equations arising in fluid mechanics and general relativity. His work addresses questions of regularity, formation of singularities, formation of black holes, and asymptotic behavior.

faculty.name: Pravesh Kothari
faculty.title: Computer Science
faculty.summary: Kothari works on algorithms and computational thresholds for average-case computational problems, random matrices, and extremal combinatorics.

faculty.name: Naomi E. Leonard
faculty.title: Mechanical & Aerospace Engineering
faculty.sub_field: Nonlinear control theory and dynamical systems
faculty.summary: Leonard works on nonlinear control theory and design, geometric mechanics, dynamical systems and feedback. Her work spans cooperative control in robotic vehicle networks, autonomous ocean sampling systems, and collective behavior analysis in animal groups and human-robot teams.

faculty.name: Simon A. Levin
faculty.title: Ecology & Evolutionary Biology
faculty.summary: Levin's research interests include spatial heterogeneity and problems of scale; dynamics of populations and communities; evolutionary, mathematical, and theoretical ecology; dynamics of disease; and ecological economics.

faculty.name: Elliott H. Lieb
faculty.title: Professor Emeritus, Mathematics / Physics
faculty.summary: Lieb works on mathematical physics with emphasis on Schroedinger operators. His interests include questions concerning stability of matter and atomic physics, quantum electrodynamics, statistical mechanics, and problems arising from condensed matter physics.

faculty.name: Luigi Martinelli
faculty.title: Mechanical & Aerospace Engineering
faculty.summary: Martinelli develops mathematical models, algorithms, and computer codes for the simulation of turbulent flows over realistic industrial configurations across subsonic, transonic, and supersonic regimes. His work also covers CFD software on modern computing platforms and multi-physics design optimization for aircraft design.

faculty.name: William A. Massey
faculty.title: Operations Research & Financial Engineering
faculty.summary: Massey's research focuses on dynamical queueing systems, communication systems and services, and the analysis of stochastic networks.

faculty.name: Assaf Naor
faculty.title: Mathematics
faculty.summary: Naor works in analysis, probability, and quantitative geometry, with applications of these areas to combinatorics, mathematical physics, and theoretical computer science.

faculty.name: Jonathan Pillow
faculty.title: Neuroscience Institute
faculty.sub_field: Computational neuroscience and statistical signal processing
faculty.summary: Pillow works in computational neuroscience and statistical signal processing, including point process regression models, latent variable models for spike train and imaging data, receptive field estimation, inference for biophysical models, spike sorting, and statistical signal processing for calcium imaging. His interests also include active learning/closed-loop experimental design, Bayesian optimization, perceptual decision making, and visual motion perception.

faculty.name: H. Vincent Poor
faculty.title: Electrical and Computer Engineering
faculty.sub_field: Information theory, machine learning and network science
faculty.summary: Poor works on information theory, machine learning and network science, with applications in wireless networks, energy systems and related areas.

faculty.name: Warren Powell
faculty.title: Professor Emeritus, Operations Research & Financial Engineering
faculty.sub_field: Stochastic optimization; energy systems and sustainability
faculty.summary: Powell is a Professor Emeritus in Operations Research & Financial Engineering. His research focuses on energy (conservation, policy and security, renewable, systems analysis, technology) and environmental economics, climate and energy, and sustainability.

faculty.name: Frans Pretorius
faculty.title: Physics
faculty.summary: Pretorius is affiliated with Princeton's Physics Department and the Program in Applied & Computational Mathematics. His research covers black holes, gravitational collapse, gravitational waves and their sources, higher dimensional gravity, numerical solution methods, and cosmology.

faculty.name: Jean-Hervé Prévost
faculty.title: Professor Emeritus, Civil & Environmental Engineering
faculty.summary: Prévost is a Professor Emeritus in Civil & Environmental Engineering. His work centers on computational solid mechanics, including wave propagation in porous media, finite element methods, crack propagation, dynamic instabilities, thermoelasticity, and reservoir modeling.

faculty.name: Herschel Rabitz
faculty.title: Chemistry
faculty.sub_field: Applied mathematics at the interface of engineering, physics, and chemistry
faculty.summary: Rabitz is in the Chemistry department. He develops applied-mathematical tools blending analytical and numerical techniques, with applications spanning optimal control theory, quantum dynamics, molecular scattering theory, chemical kinetics, and biomolecular modeling.

faculty.name: Peter J. Ramadge
faculty.title: Professor Emeritus, Electrical and Computer Engineering
faculty.sub_field: Wireless networks, social networks, and smart grid systems
faculty.summary: Ramadge is a Professor Emeritus in Electrical and Computer Engineering. His research interests focus on advances in several fields of rapid technology development, notably wireless networks, social networks and smart grid.

faculty.name: Elizaveta Rebrova
faculty.title: Operations Research & Financial Engineering
faculty.summary: Rebrova is in Operations Research & Financial Engineering. Her research focuses on high-dimensional probability, randomized algorithms, numerical linear algebra, matrix and tensor methods, mathematics of data, robust and interpretable learning, and non-asymptotic random matrix theory.

faculty.name: Jennifer Rexford
faculty.title: Computer Science
faculty.sub_field: Computer networks / Internet routing and management
faculty.summary: Rexford is in the Computer Science department. Her work focuses on Internet routing, network measurement, and network management, with the larger goal of making data networks easier to design, understand, and manage.

faculty.name: Clarence Rowley
faculty.title: Mechanical & Aerospace Engineering
faculty.sub_field: Dynamical systems and control theory with applications in fluid mechanics
faculty.summary: Rowley is in Mechanical & Aerospace Engineering. His research focuses on dynamical systems, model reduction, and control theory, especially with applications in fluid mechanics, along with numerical methods and geometric mechanics.

faculty.name: Szymon Rusinkiewicz
faculty.title: Computer Science
faculty.sub_field: Interface between computers and the visual and tangible world
faculty.summary: Rusinkiewicz is in the Computer Science department. His work focuses on the interface between computers and the visual and tangible world: acquisition, representation, analysis, and fabrication of 3D shape, motion, surface appearance, and scattering.

faculty.name: Guillermo Sapiro
faculty.title: Electrical and Computer Engineering
faculty.sub_field: Computer vision, image analysis, and machine learning
faculty.summary: Sapiro is in Electrical and Computer Engineering. His research encompasses theory and applications in computer vision, computer graphics, medical imaging, image analysis, machine learning, and ML for health.

faculty.name: Paul Seymour
faculty.title: Mathematics
faculty.summary: Seymour is in the Mathematics department. His work focuses on structural properties of graphs with certain induced subgraphs or minors forbidden.

faculty.name: Frederik Simons
faculty.title: Geosciences
faculty.sub_field: Mathematical geophysics and computational inverse problems
faculty.summary: Simons is in the Geosciences department. He applies mathematical and computational methods to the study of the solid Earth and planets, including physical properties recovered by seismic tomography, geodesy, and cross-spectral analysis of planetary gravity, topography, and magnetic fields.

faculty.name: Yakov Sinai
faculty.title: Professor Emeritus, Mathematics
faculty.summary: Sinai is a Professor Emeritus in Mathematics. His research encompasses various problems in the theory of dynamical systems, including quantum chaos, as well as conservation laws with random initial data and random coefficients, and connections with statistical mechanics.

faculty.name: Jaswinder Pal Singh
faculty.title: Computer Science
faculty.summary: Singh is in the Computer Science department. His research focuses on parallel applications and their implications for software and architectural design, and on system software and programming environments for multiprocessors.

faculty.name: Ronnie Sircar
faculty.title: Operations Research & Financial Engineering
faculty.summary: Sircar is in Operations Research & Financial Engineering. His research focuses on financial mathematics, stochastic volatility models, energy markets and power systems, credit risk, asymptotic and computational methods, portfolio optimization and stochastic control problems, and stochastic differential and mean field games.

faculty.name: Mete Soner
faculty.title: Operations Research & Financial Engineering
faculty.sub_field: Nonlinear PDEs, stochastic processes, and mathematical finance
faculty.summary: Mete Soner's research focuses on nonlinear analysis in partial differential equations, stochastic processes, and mathematical finance. He is affiliated with Princeton's Operations Research & Financial Engineering department.

faculty.name: John D. Storey
faculty.title: Molecular Biology
faculty.sub_field: Statistical methods for high-dimensional genomics data
faculty.summary: John D. Storey develops statistical methods, theory, and algorithms for high-dimensional data analysis problems in genomics and other areas of biology. His work spans gene expression profiling, next-generation sequencing, structured populations, and clinical genomics.

faculty.name: Joseph E. Subotnik
faculty.title: Chemistry
faculty.sub_field: Electronic processes in the condensed phase
faculty.summary: Joseph E. Subotnik studies electronic processes in the condensed phase, using electronic structure theory (with an emphasis on excited states), nonadiabatic dynamics, perturbation theory, and statistical mechanics. His group builds computational platforms for studying electronic relaxation, electron and energy transfer, and multilinear spectroscopy.

faculty.name: Sankaran Sundaresan
faculty.title: Emeritus, Chemical & Biological Engineering
faculty.summary: Sankaran Sundaresan, Emeritus faculty in Chemical & Biological Engineering, researches granular flows and fluid-particle flows.

faculty.name: Ludovic Tangpi
faculty.title: Operations Research & Financial Engineering
faculty.summary: Ludovic Tangpi works in financial mathematics (risk management, model uncertainty, optimal investment), stochastic analysis (stochastic control, SDEs, BSDEs, FBSDEs, probabilistic representations of parabolic/elliptic PDEs), and probability theory (optimal transportation, functional inequalities). He is affiliated with Princeton's Operations Research & Financial Engineering department.

faculty.name: Robert E. Tarjan
faculty.title: Computer Science
faculty.summary: Robert E. Tarjan's research spans data structures, graph algorithms, combinatorial optimization, computational complexity, computational geometry, and parallel algorithms. He is affiliated with Princeton's Computer Science department.

faculty.name: Corina Tarnita
faculty.title: Ecology & Evolutionary Biology
faculty.sub_field: Dynamics of complex interactions and emergent phenomena in biological systems
faculty.summary: Corina Tarnita studies the dynamics of complex interactions and emergent phenomena in biological systems, using mathematical modeling in collaboration with experimental and field ecologists, molecular biologists, and evolutionary biologists. She is affiliated with Princeton's Ecology & Evolutionary Biology department.

faculty.name: Romain Teyssier
faculty.title: Astrophysical Sciences
faculty.summary: Romain Teyssier works in computational astrophysics and fluid dynamics, with particular interest in understanding the physics of galaxy and star formation in a cosmological context. He is affiliated with Princeton's Astrophysical Sciences department.

faculty.name: Salvatore Torquato
faculty.title: Chemistry / PRISM
faculty.sub_field: Statistical mechanics, soft condensed matter, and materials science
faculty.summary: Salvatore Torquato's research spans statistical mechanics, soft condensed matter, and materials science, including crystals, quasicrystals, disordered phases of matter, jammed states, sphere packings, hyperuniform states, inverse statistical mechanics, self-assembly theory, percolation theory, and biophysics. He is affiliated with Princeton's Chemistry department and PRISM.

faculty.name: Jeroen Tromp
faculty.title: Geosciences
faculty.summary: Jeroen Tromp works in theoretical and computational seismology, including seismic tomography, numerical simulations of acoustic/elastic/poroelastic wave propagation, seismic hazard assessment, adjoint-state methods, and ultrasonic tomography. His home department is Geosciences.

faculty.name: Olga Troyanskaya
faculty.title: Computer Science / Molecular Biology
faculty.sub_field: Computational biology: gene function and biological networks
faculty.summary: Olga Troyanskaya applies computational science and statistics to study gene function and biological networks through integrated analysis of diverse biological data sources. She develops algorithms for biological signal detection in high-throughput data sets and for integrating genomic sequences, expression profiles, and proteomics. She is affiliated with Princeton's Computer Science and Molecular Biology departments.

faculty.name: Robert Vanderbei
faculty.title: Professor Emeritus, Operations Research & Financial Engineering
faculty.summary: Robert Vanderbei, Professor Emeritus in Operations Research & Financial Engineering, works on interior-point methods for constrained optimization (analysis and implementation), application of optimization to problems with constraints in the Fourier-transform domain, and designing high-contrast imaging systems to search for extrasolar planets.

faculty.name: Matt Weinberg
faculty.title: Computer Science
faculty.summary: Matt Weinberg works on algorithmic mechanism design (algorithm design in settings where users have their own incentives), algorithmic game theory, algorithms under uncertainty, and theoretical computer science. He is affiliated with Princeton's Computer Science department.

faculty.name: Andrea Bertozzi
faculty.title: Professor of Mathematics; Director of Applied Mathematics; Betsy Wood Knapp Chair for Innovation and Creativity
faculty.summary: Bertozzi is a leader in applied mathematics, directing UCLA's applied program. Her research spans nonlinear partial differential equations, fluid dynamics of thin films, and data science. Recent work develops graph-based and PDE methods for machine learning and image classification, models of aggregation and swarming, particle-laden and thin-film flows, and mathematical approaches to crime modelling and social dynamics. A hallmark is connecting rigorous PDE and variational analysis to real applications, including semi-supervised learning on large graphs, hyperspectral image analysis, and cooperative control of robotic swarms.

faculty.name: Terence Tao
faculty.title: Professor of Mathematics (James and Carol Collins Chair)
faculty.summary: Tao is one of the most influential pure mathematicians, working across harmonic analysis, analytic and additive number theory, combinatorics, random matrix theory and nonlinear PDE. His work includes results on prime patterns, the structure of arithmetic sets, universality for random matrices, and regularity and blow-up questions for dispersive and fluid equations. Recent research spans problems in analytic number theory, combinatorial analysis, and, increasingly, the use of formal proof assistants and AI-assisted tools in mathematics. He is known for building bridges between seemingly distant areas and for prolific collaboration.

faculty.name: Marcus Roper
faculty.title: Professor of Mathematics and Computational Medicine
faculty.summary: Roper applies mathematical modelling and fluid dynamics to understand how cells and organisms solve physical challenges. His group studies transport in fungal mycelial networks, blood flow and microcirculation, spore dispersal, and the physics of microbial life, combining asymptotic analysis, PDE modelling and close collaboration with experimentalists. Recent work examines optimality and self-organisation in biological transport networks, red-blood-cell partitioning in microvasculature, and quantitative modelling of fungal biology. His research links detailed biological data to tractable mathematical models revealing design principles of living systems.

faculty.name: Mason Porter
faculty.title: Professor of Mathematics
faculty.summary: Porter works in applied mathematics on networks, complex systems and nonlinear dynamics. His research develops methods for multilayer and temporal networks, community detection, dynamical processes on networks, and topological data analysis, with applications ranging from physical and biological systems to social science. Recent work studies opinion and information spreading on social networks, models of contagion, and structure in data from the physical, biological and information sciences. He emphasises mathematically principled tools for uncovering structure and dynamics in complex, interconnected systems and connecting them to empirical data.

faculty.name: Deanna Needell
faculty.title: Professor of Mathematics; Dunn Family Endowed Chair
faculty.summary: Needell works in computational and applied mathematics at the interface of signal processing, optimization and machine learning. Her research develops and analyses efficient algorithms for compressed sensing, sparse recovery, randomized numerical linear algebra, stochastic iterative methods, and nonnegative matrix factorization, with rigorous theoretical guarantees. Recent work addresses large-scale and online optimization, topic modelling and interpretable machine learning, and applications to medical imaging and social-good problems. She combines probabilistic and functional-analytic tools with practical algorithm design for high-dimensional data.

faculty.name: Rowan Killip
faculty.title: Professor of Mathematics
faculty.summary: Killip works in analysis, spectral theory, and nonlinear dispersive partial differential equations. With frequent collaborator Monica Visan he has advanced the well-posedness and long-time behavior theory for equations such as the nonlinear Schrodinger and Korteweg-de Vries equations, including sharp results at critical regularity and on the role of conserved quantities. He also studies spectral and inverse-spectral theory of Schrodinger and Jacobi operators, orthogonal polynomials, and random operators. He was invited to speak at the 2026 International Congress of Mathematicians.

faculty.name: Monica Vișan
faculty.title: Professor of Mathematics
faculty.summary: Visan studies nonlinear dispersive partial differential equations, especially the nonlinear Schrodinger and Korteweg-de Vries equations. She is known for resolving critical well-posedness and scattering problems, treating equations on domains with boundaries, and building invariant measures and low-regularity theory using tools from harmonic analysis and, more recently, completely integrable structure. Her method of commuting flows has produced sharp global results. Named a 2026 ICM invited speaker and AWM-AMS Emmy Noether Lecturer, she frequently collaborates with Rowan Killip.

faculty.name: Chandrashekhar Khare
faculty.title: Professor and Chair of Mathematics
faculty.summary: Khare works in algebraic number theory, focusing on Galois representations and their links to modular and automorphic forms. With Jean-Pierre Wintenberger he proved Serre's modularity conjecture, work recognized by the 2011 Cole Prize in Number Theory. His research addresses modularity lifting, deformation theory of Galois representations, and reciprocity between arithmetic and automorphy. He currently serves as chair of the UCLA Department of Mathematics. Recent work continues to explore modularity, class field theory analogues, and the arithmetic of elliptic curves.

faculty.name: Ko Honda
faculty.title: Professor of Mathematics
faculty.summary: Honda works in contact and symplectic geometry, low-dimensional topology, and their connections to dynamics and mathematical physics. He developed convex surface theory and classification results for tight contact structures on three-manifolds, and contributed to the foundations of contact homology, Heegaard Floer theory, and bordered invariants. His research links pseudo-holomorphic curve techniques with the topology of three- and four-manifolds. Recent work advances higher-dimensional contact topology and functorial, sheaf-theoretic approaches to Floer-theoretic invariants of manifolds with boundary.

faculty.name: Sucharit Sarkar
faculty.title: Professor of Mathematics
faculty.summary: Sarkar works in low-dimensional topology, focusing on knot and link invariants and the homological algebra behind them. With collaborators he constructed a stable homotopy refinement of Khovanov homology, giving a space-level invariant of links, and developed combinatorial and computational approaches to Heegaard Floer homology. His research probes relationships between gauge-theoretic, symplectic, and combinatorial invariants of knots, three-manifolds, and four-manifolds. Recent work studies functoriality, spectral refinements, and structural properties of Khovanov and Floer homology theories.

faculty.name: Burt Totaro
faculty.title: Professor of Mathematics
faculty.summary: Totaro works in algebraic geometry, often bringing tools from topology and homotopy theory to bear on cycles, cohomology, and moduli. He is known for foundational contributions to the Chow ring of classifying spaces, the study of algebraic cycles and their torsion, and questions of rationality and stable rationality of algebraic varieties. His research also spans Hodge theory, the geometry of Fano varieties, and cohomology of algebraic groups. Recent work examines torsion algebraic cycles and obstructions to rationality.

faculty.name: Alexander Merkurjev
faculty.title: Professor of Mathematics
faculty.summary: Merkurjev works in algebra, especially algebraic K-theory, quadratic forms, and cohomological invariants of algebraic groups. His celebrated theorem with Suslin relating the Brauer group to K-theory transformed the field and underpinned later proofs of the Milnor and Bloch-Kato conjectures. He studies central simple algebras, essential dimension, motivic cohomology, and Galois cohomology of linear algebraic groups. A recipient of the AMS Cole Prize in Algebra, he continues research on essential dimension and cohomological invariants.

faculty.name: Igor Pak
faculty.title: Professor of Mathematics
faculty.summary: Pak works in combinatorics and its interactions with probability, algebra, and computational complexity. His research spans enumerative and bijective combinatorics, partition theory, combinatorial inequalities, and the complexity of counting problems, including which combinatorial quantities admit efficient formulas. He has studied random generation, tilings, integer points in polytopes, and the algorithmic hardness underlying log-concavity and unimodality phenomena. Recent work probes combinatorial inequalities from an algebraic and probabilistic viewpoint and their computational-complexity aspects, connecting enumeration to questions in theoretical computer science.

faculty.name: Itay Neeman
faculty.title: Professor of Mathematics
faculty.summary: Neeman is a set theorist working on inner model theory, determinacy, forcing, and large cardinals. He has made major contributions connecting the strength of determinacy axioms to inner models with Woodin cardinals, and developed techniques for iteration trees and long games. His research also treats forcing constructions, the tree property, and combinatorial set theory. A Simons Fellow and recipient of the Hausdorff Medal, he is affiliated with the UCLA Logic Center and mentors students in mathematical logic.

faculty.name: Inwon Kim
faculty.title: Professor of Mathematics
faculty.summary: Kim studies partial differential equations, with emphasis on free boundary problems and nonlinear evolution equations arising in physics and biology. Her work analyzes existence, regularity, and asymptotic behavior for models of fluid flow, phase transitions, crowd motion, and tumor growth, including connections between porous-medium and Hele-Shaw type limits. She uses viscosity solution methods, optimal transport, and gradient-flow techniques. Recent research treats aggregation-diffusion equations, congestion models, and the emergence of interfaces in nonlinear diffusion.

faculty.name: Wilfrid Gangbo
faculty.title: Professor of Mathematics
faculty.summary: Gangbo works in the calculus of variations, nonlinear partial differential equations, and optimal transportation. He is known for foundational results on the existence and structure of optimal transport maps for general cost functions, and for applying transport ideas to fluid mechanics, kinetic theory, and mean field games. His research develops Hamilton-Jacobi equations on spaces of measures and Wasserstein geometry. A recipient of the 2026 AMS Award for Distinguished Public Service, he continues work on high-dimensional mean field problems.

faculty.name: Stanley Osher
faculty.title: Professor of Mathematics; Director of Special Projects, IPAM
faculty.summary: Osher is a leader in numerical analysis and scientific computing whose methods are used across physics, imaging, and data science. He co-invented level set methods for evolving interfaces, ENO and WENO shock-capturing schemes for hyperbolic conservation laws, and total-variation-based models for image denoising and reconstruction. His work also spans fast optimization for sparse and compressed sensing problems and Hamilton-Jacobi equations. Director of Special Projects at IPAM, he continues developing algorithms linking PDEs, optimization, and machine learning.

faculty.name: Guido Montúfar
faculty.title: Associate Professor of Mathematics and Statistics & Data Science
faculty.summary: Montufar develops the mathematical foundations of machine learning, leading the Mathematical Machine Learning Group at UCLA and the Max Planck Institute for Mathematics in the Sciences. His research analyzes the expressive power of deep neural networks, the geometry of their function spaces and loss landscapes, and the dynamics of training and optimization. He draws on information geometry, algebraic statistics, and optimal transport to understand generalization and representation. A Sloan Fellow, his recent work studies gradient dynamics, implicit bias, and reinforcement learning theory.

faculty.name: Marek Biskup
faculty.title: Professor of Mathematics
faculty.summary: Biskup works in probability theory and mathematical statistical mechanics. His research studies the large-scale behavior of disordered and interacting systems, including phase transitions, random walks in random environments, and models of magnetism and percolation. He has made notable contributions to the extremal theory of the two-dimensional discrete Gaussian free field and to random conductance models. He leads the UCLA probability group. Recent work analyzes extreme values, local times, and scaling limits of log-correlated random fields.

faculty.name: Luminita Vese
faculty.title: Professor of Mathematics
faculty.summary: Vese works in applied mathematics, developing variational and partial-differential-equation methods for image processing and computer vision. She is known for active-contour and region-based models for image segmentation, including widely used level-set formulations building on the Mumford-Shah functional, as well as methods for image denoising, decomposition into cartoon and texture, and restoration. Her research applies these tools to medical and scientific imaging. Recent work advances variational models, numerical schemes, and multiscale representations for image analysis and reconstruction.

faculty.name: Eric Cytrynbaum
faculty.title: Professor of Mathematics
faculty.summary: Cytrynbaum works in mathematical and computational cell biology, studying how cells organise themselves in space and time. His research uses ODE/PDE models, dynamical systems and simulation to understand the cytoskeleton, mitotic spindle positioning, bacterial cell division and pattern formation of intracellular structures. Recent work addresses self-organisation of protein systems, microtubule dynamics, and geometry-sensing mechanisms in cells, often in collaboration with experimental biophysicists. He emphasises mechanistic models that connect molecular-scale interactions to emergent cellular-scale spatial organisation and testable biological predictions.

faculty.name: Daniel Coombs
faculty.title: Professor of Mathematics; Head, Department of Mathematics
faculty.summary: Coombs applies mathematics to immunology, infectious disease and cell biophysics. His research models the dynamics of immune receptors and T-cell recognition, within-host and population-level dynamics of viral infections such as HIV, and the statistical analysis of single-particle tracking data to infer molecular motion on cell surfaces. Recent work spans epidemiological modelling, quantitative analysis of membrane receptor organisation, and stochastic models linking molecular events to cellular decisions. He combines PDE, stochastic-process and statistical methods with close collaboration between mathematics, immunology and physics.

faculty.name: Michael J. Ward
faculty.title: Professor of Mathematics
faculty.summary: Ward is an applied mathematician specialising in singular perturbation theory and the analysis of localized patterns in PDEs. His research develops matched asymptotic and hybrid analytical-numerical methods to study spot, spike and stripe solutions of reaction-diffusion systems, narrow-escape and first-passage problems, and dynamics of concentrated structures relevant to chemistry and biology. Recent work analyses pattern formation, stability and dynamics of localized states in models such as Gierer-Meinhardt and Gray-Scott, and diffusion in domains with small traps. His work provides sharp asymptotic understanding of strongly nonlinear pattern-forming systems.

faculty.name: James J. Feng
faculty.title: Professor of Mathematics and of Chemical and Biological Engineering
faculty.summary: Feng works in the modelling and computation of complex fluids and biological flows. His research develops continuum and computational models for viscoelastic and multiphase fluids, moving interfaces, and the mechanics of cells and tissues, combining PDE modelling with numerical simulation. Recent work addresses cell migration and morphogenesis, biofilm and mucus dynamics, droplet and interface behaviour, and fluid-structure interactions in physiological systems. He bridges applied mathematics and chemical/biological engineering, using quantitative models to illuminate the physics of soft biological and industrial materials.

faculty.name: Leah Edelstein-Keshet
faculty.title: Professor Emerita of Mathematics
faculty.summary: Edelstein-Keshet is a pioneer of mathematical biology and author of a classic textbook in the field; she is now Professor Emerita but remains research-active and was awarded the 2025 CRM-Fields-PIMS Prize. Her work models cell polarization, motility and shape change, the reaction-diffusion dynamics of Rho GTPase signalling, and collective movement in cell and animal groups. She develops PDE and ODE models tightly linked to experiments, revealing mechanisms of pattern formation and coordinated motion. As emerita she may have limited capacity to take on new PhD students.

requirements.english: Proof of English: TOEFL iBT >= 79 (or paper >= 550), or IELTS >= 6.0, or German Abitur with English to at least B2; program is taught in English and no German is required.
requirements.admission_model_note: Taught two-year master's; admission is decided by the department's examination board on the basis of a qualifying bachelor's (at least 120 ECTS from mathematics modules and overall grade of 2.5 or better on the German scale). Thesis supervision is arranged later within the Hausdorff Center / BIGS-M ecosystem.

funding.note: No tuition fees — only a ~€324 semester social contribution (covers a transit ticket). Master's students are generally self-funded for living costs; external scholarships (e.g. DAAD, Deutschlandstipendium) are available.

requirements.contact_note: Coursework-based admission; pre-application contact with professors is not required.

faculty.name: Peter Scholze
faculty.title: Professor of Mathematics (Hausdorff Chair)
faculty.summary: Scholze is a Fields Medalist and one of the leading figures in arithmetic geometry, based in Bonn and affiliated with the Max Planck Institute for Mathematics. His work created the theory of perfectoid spaces and reshaped p-adic geometry and the p-adic Langlands program, with tools such as prismatic cohomology and diamonds. More recently, together with collaborators, he has developed condensed mathematics, a framework unifying algebra and topology, and pursued its analytic and geometric consequences. His research connects number theory, representation theory and algebraic geometry at a foundational level.

faculty.name: Stefan Schwede
faculty.title: Professor of Mathematics
faculty.summary: Schwede is a leading algebraic topologist working in stable and equivariant homotopy theory. His research develops the foundations and structural theory of spectra, symmetric and orthogonal spectra, and global equivariant homotopy theory, which treats compatible actions of all compact Lie groups simultaneously. Recent work includes systematic accounts of global homotopy theory and applications to equivariant stable homotopy, using categorical and model-theoretic frameworks. His research provides organising principles and computational tools that underpin much of modern homotopy theory and its connections to algebra and geometry.

faculty.name: Herbert Koch
faculty.title: Professor of Mathematics
faculty.summary: Koch is an analyst specialising in nonlinear partial differential equations and harmonic analysis. His research studies well-posedness, regularity and long-time behaviour for dispersive and parabolic equations, including Schrödinger, KdV and wave-type equations, often at low regularity and in connection with integrable structure. Recent work addresses conserved energies and sharp well-posedness for dispersive models, quasilinear problems, and interactions between harmonic analysis and PDE. He develops refined analytic techniques for controlling nonlinear interactions and understanding the fine structure of solutions to fundamental evolution equations.

faculty.name: Karl-Theodor Sturm
faculty.title: Professor of Mathematics
faculty.summary: Sturm works at the interface of probability, analysis and geometry. He is a founder of the synthetic theory of Ricci curvature bounds for metric measure spaces via optimal transport, and studies heat flow, Dirichlet forms and functional inequalities in singular geometric settings. Recent research addresses metric measure geometry, gradient flows, distances between geometric spaces, and stochastic analysis on spaces with curvature bounds, including random geometry and geometric aspects of optimal transport. His work links probabilistic tools, geometric analysis and the theory of nonsmooth spaces.

requirements.english: TOEFL (typ. iBT 100) or IELTS (typ. 7.0), Cambridge English, or Duolingo; waived for native speakers or a recent degree from an English-medium institution in the US/UK/Ireland/Canada/Australia/NZ.
requirements.admission_model_note: Applicants are admitted by a departmental admissions committee via holistic review routed by stated area of interest; students typically identify a research advisor during the first year through lab visits and research assistantships rather than being matched at admission.

funding.note: All PhD students are fully supported for the program's duration with tuition, a living stipend, and health insurance via fellowships and research/teaching assistantships.

requirements.contact_note: Admission is by committee; contacting individual faculty before applying is not required and does not affect the decision.

faculty.name: Pablo Jarillo-Herrero
faculty.title: Cecil and Ida Green Professor of Physics
faculty.summary: Jarillo-Herrero pioneered 'twistronics,' discovering superconductivity and correlated insulating states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene. Recent work (2024-2025) measured the superfluid stiffness of magic-angle twisted bilayer and trilayer graphene, revealing unconventional pairing, and explored topological superconductivity and quantum-geometric effects in moiré systems. His group also demonstrated on-chip multi-degree-of-freedom control of two-dimensional materials and studied plasmons and correlated phases in engineered van der Waals heterostructures. He was named a 2024 Clarivate Citation Laureate for this work.

faculty.name: Senthil Todadri
faculty.title: William and Emma Rogers Professor of Physics
faculty.summary: Senthil develops theories of strongly correlated quantum matter beyond the Landau paradigm, including quantum spin liquids, deconfined quantum criticality, and non-Fermi-liquid metals. His recent work applies these ideas to moiré heterostructures, predicting ferromagnetism and quantum anomalous Hall effects later observed in twisted graphene experiments, and to the correlated and superconducting phases of magic-angle graphene. He continues to study continuous Mott transitions, fractionalized Fermi liquids, and the interplay of topology, gauge structure, and criticality in two-dimensional electron systems.

faculty.name: Wolfgang Ketterle
faculty.title: John D. MacArthur Professor of Physics
faculty.summary: Ketterle, a 2001 Nobel laureate for Bose-Einstein condensation, studies ultracold atomic gases, superfluidity, spin physics, and ultracold molecules. Recent work (2024) realized a bilayer system of dipolar atoms separated by roughly 50 nanometers, probing dipolar interactions at unprecedented length scales. His group has investigated coherent and incoherent light scattering by single-atom wavepackets, probed quantum many-body dynamics via subsystem Loschmidt echoes, and developed high-density magneto-optical trapping of calcium monofluoride molecules for studies of ultracold chemistry and quantum simulation.

faculty.name: Nergis Mavalvala
faculty.title: Curtis and Kathleen Marble Professor of Astrophysics; Dean of the School of Science
faculty.summary: Mavalvala works on gravitational-wave detection with LIGO and on quantum measurement science. She and collaborators developed and deployed frequency-dependent squeezed light in LIGO, and in 2024 reported squeezing the detectors' quantum noise below the standard quantum limit, broadening sensitivity across the astrophysical frequency band. Her group also explores macroscopic quantum effects and optomechanical squeezing to prepare and measure mechanical oscillators near their quantum ground state, extending the reach of gravitational-wave observatories. She serves as Dean of MIT's School of Science.

faculty.name: Tracy Slatyer
faculty.title: Professor of Physics; Director, MIT Center for Theoretical Physics
faculty.summary: Slatyer is a theoretical astrophysicist searching for signatures of dark matter in astrophysical and cosmological data. She co-discovered the 'Fermi bubbles,' giant gamma-ray structures above and below the galactic plane. Recent work develops precision predictions for photon signals from annihilating dark matter, models dark-sector forces and their imprint on the early universe and cosmic microwave background, and applies data-analysis and machine-learning methods to gamma-ray observations of the Galactic Center. She directs the MIT Center for Theoretical Physics.

faculty.name: Or Hen
faculty.title: Associate Professor of Physics
faculty.summary: Hen studies short-range correlations (SRCs) in atomic nuclei: fleeting, high-momentum neutron-proton pairs probed by high-energy electron, photon, proton, and ion scattering. His group has linked SRCs to the nuclear EMC effect, connecting nucleon-structure modifications to two-nucleon dynamics, and extended measurements to neutrino scattering and dense nuclear matter. Recent work (2024-2025) measured SRCs via bremsstrahlung gamma-ray emission in heavy-ion collisions and examined three-body correlations and their consequences for the neutron-star equation of state.

faculty.name: Soonwon Choi
faculty.title: Victor F. Weisskopf Associate Professor of Physics
faculty.summary: Choi is a theorist studying far-from-equilibrium dynamics of strongly interacting quantum many-body systems and their applications to quantum information. He predicted and helped observe the emergence of universal random-state ensembles ('deep thermalization') under natural Hamiltonian dynamics, enabling efficient benchmarking of quantum simulators via many-body quantum chaos. His recent work analyzes measurement-induced phase transitions in the dynamics of quantum information and designs protocols for quantum sensing, simulation, and error correction using programmable atom arrays and other platforms.

faculty.name: Nikta Fakhri
faculty.title: Professor of Physics
faculty.summary: Fakhri leads the Physics of Living Systems group, studying active, non-equilibrium matter from molecules to cells to whole organisms. Her group uses starfish oocytes and embryos as model systems to reveal how microscopic, energy-consuming fluctuations produce macroscopic symmetry breaking, including odd elasticity and chiral 'active crystals' of spinning embryos. She pioneered fluorescent single-walled carbon nanotubes as probes of intracellular mechanics and develops theoretical frameworks connecting broken time-reversal symmetry, entropy production, and pattern formation in living matter.

faculty.name: Anna Frebel
faculty.title: Professor of Physics, Division Head for Astrophysics
faculty.summary: Frebel practices 'stellar archaeology,' using high-resolution spectroscopy of the oldest, most metal-poor stars in the Milky Way halo and nearby dwarf galaxies to reconstruct chemical conditions in the early universe. Her measurements of individual stars over 12 billion years old constrain the first stars, supernova nucleosynthesis yields, and the r-process that forges heavy elements. Recent work characterizes r-process-enhanced stars and dwarf-galaxy chemical evolution, probing early star formation and the assembly history of the Galaxy and its satellites.

faculty.name: Liang Fu
faculty.title: Professor of Physics
faculty.summary: Fu is a condensed matter theorist known for co-predicting topological crystalline insulators and advancing the theory of topological superconductivity and Majorana states. His recent work explores fractional quantum anomalous Hall states and correlated phases in moire and twisted transition-metal-dichalcogenide bilayers, the role of quantum geometry and Berry curvature in flat-band physics, and unconventional superconductivity. He also develops ideas connecting band topology, ferroelectricity, and nonlinear optical and transport responses in quantum materials for potential device applications.

faculty.name: Joseph Checkelsky
faculty.title: Professor of Physics
faculty.summary: Checkelsky's group synthesizes and measures crystalline quantum materials to uncover exotic electronic states arising from topology and geometric frustration. His team pioneered kagome-lattice metals hosting flat electronic bands and recently reported realizing a flat band in a three-dimensional crystal, a route toward strong correlations and possible superconductivity. Recent work includes evidence of striped electronic phases in structurally modulated superlattices and studies linking flat bands, strange-metal behavior, and the Kondo effect, aiming to engineer materials with tailored quantum functionality.

faculty.name: Martin Zwierlein
faculty.title: Thomas A. Frank (1977) Professor of Physics
faculty.summary: Zwierlein studies strongly interacting ultracold Fermi gases as tunable analogs of complex quantum matter. His group uses quantum gas microscopy to image individual fermionic atoms in optical lattices, probing Hubbard-model physics, pairing, and transport relevant to high-temperature superconductivity. Recent efforts include creating and cooling ultracold polar molecules toward molecular quantum computing and simulation, measuring universal thermodynamics and spin transport in unitary Fermi gases, and directly visualizing pairing and magnetic correlations to test theories of correlated fermion systems.

faculty.name: Vladan Vuletic
faculty.title: Lester Wolfe Professor of Physics
faculty.summary: Vuletic works at the interface of quantum optics and quantum information with atoms and light. His group generates spin-squeezed and entangled atomic ensembles to push optical atomic clocks and sensors beyond the standard quantum limit. Working with neutral-atom and Rydberg-array platforms, his collaborations have demonstrated programmable quantum simulators and, more recently, logical qubits and error-corrected operations in reconfigurable atom arrays. He also studies strong photon-photon interactions mediated by atoms, building toward scalable quantum networks and computation.

faculty.name: Sara Seager
faculty.title: Professor of Physics; Professor of Aeronautics and Astronautics; Class of 1941 Professor of Planetary Science
faculty.summary: Seager is a leader in exoplanet science, pioneering theory of exoplanet atmospheres, interiors, and the search for signs of life on worlds beyond the Solar System. She develops frameworks for identifying atmospheric biosignature gases and studies how starlight interacts with planetary atmospheres. She has led and contributed to space missions including TESS and small satellites, and continues designing concepts for directly imaging Earth-like planets. Recent work spans candidate biosignatures, exoplanet atmosphere characterization, and instrumentation for future missions to detect habitable environments.

faculty.name: Erin Kara
faculty.title: Associate Professor of Physics
faculty.summary: Kara is an observational astrophysicist studying how black holes grow and shape their surroundings. She advanced X-ray reverberation mapping, using time lags between X-ray light echoes off infalling gas to map accretion flows and probe strongly curved spacetime near event horizons. Her group analyzes black hole X-ray binaries, active galactic nuclei, tidal disruption events, and quasi-periodic eruptions using missions such as NICER. She serves as deputy principal investigator for the proposed AXIS X-ray probe mission concept targeting a 2030s launch.

faculty.name: Iain Stewart
faculty.title: Otto (1939) and Jane Morningstar Professor of Science
faculty.summary: Stewart is a theoretical particle physicist and a founder of soft-collinear effective theory, a framework for describing energetic quarks and gluons in QCD. His research develops precision predictions for collider observables at the LHC, including jet substructure, event shapes, and factorization theorems that separate physics across energy scales. Recent work refines high-precision extractions of Standard Model parameters such as the strong coupling and top-quark mass, and applies effective field theory methods to jets, resummation, and searches for new physics.

faculty.name: Phiala Shanahan
faculty.title: Professor of Physics
faculty.summary: Shanahan is a nuclear and particle theorist using lattice quantum chromodynamics to compute the structure of hadrons and light nuclei from first principles. She pioneers physics-informed machine learning, embedding gauge and spacetime symmetries into generative models to sample high-dimensional lattice field-theory distributions far more efficiently than conventional methods. Her group achieved early calculations of the gluon structure of nuclei and studies the origin of nuclear properties, supporting interpretation of experiments at facilities including the future Electron-Ion Collider.

faculty.name: Janet Conrad
faculty.title: Professor of Physics
faculty.summary: Conrad is an experimental particle physicist searching for new physics in the neutrino sector. She has led and contributed to accelerator and detector experiments including MiniBooNE, MicroBooNE, and IceCube, investigating anomalies that could signal light sterile neutrinos beyond the three known flavors. Her group develops the IsoDAR concept, a compact cyclotron-driven decay-at-rest source designed for definitive sterile-neutrino and precision electroweak searches. Recent work spans global fits to oscillation data, detector R&D, and interpretation of persistent short-baseline anomalies.

faculty.name: William Oliver
faculty.title: Professor of Physics; Henry Ellis Warren (1894) Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science
faculty.summary: Oliver leads MIT's Engineering Quantum Systems group, developing superconducting qubits and the materials, fabrication, and control systems needed for scalable quantum processors. His team studies coherence-limiting noise, high-fidelity gates, and architectures for modular and chiplet-based quantum computers. Recent work demonstrated commensurate-pulse control that suppresses counter-rotating errors in low-frequency fluxonium qubits, enabling faster, more accurate operations, and advanced fast, high-fidelity two-qubit gates. He also directs MIT quantum-engineering initiatives bridging campus and Lincoln Laboratory toward fault-tolerant quantum computing.

faculty.name: Jeff Gore
faculty.title: Professor of Physics
faculty.summary: Gore applies quantitative experimental and theoretical physics to living systems, using laboratory microbial communities as tractable models of ecology and evolution. His group tests theories of population dynamics, cooperation, and cheating, mapping how interactions produce stability, tipping points, and early-warning signals before ecosystem collapse. Recent work explores how diversity, coexistence, and emergent phases arise in communities of many species, drawing analogies to statistical-physics phase transitions and probing rules that govern assembly, resilience, and evolutionary dynamics in complex biological systems.

faculty.name: Miklos Porkolab
faculty.title: Professor of Physics, Post-Tenure
faculty.summary: Porkolab is a plasma physicist focused on magnetically confined fusion and the fundamental physics of hot plasmas. He founded and long directed MIT's Plasma Science and Fusion Center research on wave-plasma interactions, radio-frequency heating and current drive, parametric instabilities, and turbulence-driven transport in tokamaks. His group develops advanced microwave and laser scattering diagnostics to measure plasma fluctuations, validating turbulence models on devices such as Alcator C-Mod and DIII-D and informing the physics basis for burning-plasma experiments including ITER and compact high-field fusion concepts.

faculty.name: Mete Atatüre
faculty.title: Professor of Physics (Head of Department)
faculty.summary: Atatüre leads the Quantum Information and Control group and is Head of the Cavendish. His experimental work builds light-matter quantum interfaces in solids for quantum-network hardware, using single spins in semiconductor quantum dots and colour centres in diamond and hexagonal boron nitride. Recent efforts focus on optically active spin qubits and single-photon sources in atomically thin 2D materials and van der Waals heterostructures, nanoscale quantum sensing and imaging, and generating spin-photon entanglement for distributed quantum communication.

faculty.name: Suchitra Sebastian
faculty.title: Professor of Physics
faculty.summary: Sebastian leads the Fundamental Physics of Quantum Matter group, creating and probing complex correlated materials under extreme conditions of ultra-low temperature, intense magnetic fields, and high pressure. Using quantum-oscillation and transport measurements, her recent work has uncovered an unconventional insulating state that unexpectedly displays metal-like quantum oscillations, explored unconventional and high-temperature superconductivity, and searched for exotic emergent phases in Kondo insulators and strongly correlated electron systems. She was awarded the 2022 New Horizons in Physics Prize for this research.

faculty.name: Claudio Castelnovo
faculty.title: Professor of Theoretical Physics
faculty.summary: Castelnovo is a Professor of Theoretical Physics in the Theory of Condensed Matter group. His research addresses emergent and out-of-equilibrium phenomena in strongly correlated many-body systems, notably frustrated magnets and spin ice, where he helped predict emergent magnetic monopoles. Recent work spans the slow relaxation and dynamics of spin-ice materials, fractionalised excitations and topological order, quantum spin liquids, and how disorder and non-equilibrium driving shape quantum matter, increasingly connecting these ideas to quantum simulation and quantum information.

faculty.name: Roberto Maiolino
faculty.title: Professor of Experimental Astrophysics
faculty.summary: Maiolino is Professor of Experimental Astrophysics and a Royal Society Research Professor studying galaxy formation and the growth of supermassive black holes in the early Universe. He co-leads JWST-NIRSpec guaranteed-time surveys and has recently reported some of the earliest and most distant galaxies and black holes yet found, including candidate direct-collapse black holes and unexpectedly chemically enriched primordial systems. His group also works on galaxy chemical evolution, outflows and star-formation quenching, and instrumentation for JWST, the VLT and the ELT.

faculty.name: Paula Álvarez Cartelle
faculty.title: Associate Professor
faculty.summary: Álvarez Cartelle is an Associate Professor in the High Energy Physics group and a member of the LHCb collaboration at CERN's Large Hadron Collider. Her research centres on precision tests of the Standard Model through rare b-quark decays, particularly b to s(d) dilepton transitions that probe lepton-flavour universality and potential new physics. She led Cambridge's LHCb team from 2022 to 2025 and works on flavour-physics measurements and detector operations exploiting the high-statistics datasets delivered by LHC Run 3.

faculty.name: Akshay Rao
faculty.title: Professor of Physics
faculty.summary: Rao is a Professor of Physics leading optoelectronics and energy-materials research at the Cavendish and Maxwell Centre. His group uses ultrafast optical spectroscopy and microscopy to map electronic, structural and transport dynamics in organic semiconductors, metal-halide perovskites and other energy materials with high spatial and temporal precision. Recent work includes singlet fission for enhanced photovoltaics, long-range triplet and charge transport, and photon multiplication; he co-founded Cambridge Photon Technology and Illumion to commercialise these advances.

faculty.name: Sarah Bohndiek
faculty.title: Professor of Biomedical Physics
faculty.summary: Bohndiek is Professor of Biomedical Physics, jointly appointed with the CRUK Cambridge Institute, and leads the VISION lab within the Physics of Life theme. Her group develops low-cost optics and photonics for early cancer detection, especially photoacoustic imaging and hyperspectral endoscopy to interrogate tumour vasculature, oxygenation and the microenvironment. Recent efforts translate these methods toward the clinic, including endoscopic detection of oesophageal disease, and use imaging to track tumour evolution and metabolic changes during cancer progression.

faculty.name: Jeremy Baumberg
faculty.title: Harold Aspden Professor of Fundamental Physics
faculty.summary: Baumberg, the Harold Aspden Professor of Fundamental Physics, directs the NanoPhotonics Centre and the NanoDTC. His group studies strong light-matter coupling at the nanoscale, using plasmonic nanostructures and 'picocavities' that confine light to sub-nanometre volumes for single-molecule and single-atom spectroscopy and chemistry. Recent work spans molecular optomechanics, real-time SERS tracking of chemical reactions, tunable nanoparticle-on-mirror architectures, self-assembled metamaterials, and scalable approaches to nanophotonic devices, bridging fundamental optics with applications in sensing, catalysis and energy.

faculty.name: Siân Dutton
faculty.title: Professor of Physics and Solid-State Chemistry
faculty.summary: Dutton is a Professor of Physics and Solid-State Chemistry in the Quantum Matter group and Director of the Winton Programme for the Physics of Sustainability. Her multidisciplinary group synthesises and characterises functional inorganic materials, linking composition and structure to physical properties. Recent research targets energy materials, including new cathodes for lithium- and sodium-ion batteries, alongside geometrically frustrated magnets, hybrid perovskites, and low-temperature magnetocaloric materials for magnetic refrigeration, combining crystal chemistry with magnetometry, neutron scattering and low-temperature measurements.

faculty.name: Nicola Marzari
faculty.title: Cavendish Professor of Physics
faculty.summary: Marzari, elected Cavendish Professor of Physics, is a computational condensed-matter physicist developing electronic-structure theory, transport methods, and data-driven materials discovery. His group builds first-principles quantum-mechanical simulations to predict and design the properties of complex materials, pioneering maximally-localized Wannier functions and open infrastructures such as Quantum ESPRESSO, AiiDA, and the Materials Cloud. Recent work integrates machine learning and AI into high-throughput screening for energy materials, topological insulators, and two-dimensional systems. He received the 2026 APS David Adler Award in Materials Physics.

faculty.name: Henning Sirringhaus
faculty.title: Hitachi Professor of Electron Device Physics
faculty.summary: Sirringhaus, Hitachi Professor of Electron Device Physics and a Royal Society Research Professor, leads the Optoelectronics group studying charge and spin transport and photophysics of organic and solution-processed inorganic semiconductors, including halide perovskites. Recent work uses field-induced electron spin resonance to probe spin-charge dynamics, and examines non-equilibrium transport in polymer mixed ionic-electronic conductors at ultrahigh charge densities. His group targets spin relaxation, spin-to-charge conversion, and doping strategies that improve organic semiconductor performance for flexible electronics, spintronics, and bioelectronic devices.

faculty.name: Zoran Hadzibabic
faculty.title: Professor of Physics
faculty.summary: Hadzibabic leads an AMOP experimental group using ultracold nanokelvin quantum gases in optical box traps as clean, homogeneous platforms for many-body physics. Interests span superfluidity, reduced dimensionality, and far-from-equilibrium dynamics. Recent Nature work established a universal equation of state for wave turbulence in a quantum gas, alongside studies of turbulent cascades, driven disordered gases, and universal coarsening. The box-trap approach simplifies comparison with theory and enables qualitatively new experiments on non-equilibrium phenomena that remain hard to understand elsewhere.

faculty.name: Ulrich Keyser
faculty.title: Professor of Applied Physics
faculty.summary: Keyser, Professor of Applied Physics, works at the interface of physics, chemistry, and the life sciences, developing single-molecule sensing with solid-state and DNA nanopores. His group engineers digitally encoded DNA nanostructures and dumbbell nanoswitches for highly multiplexed detection of nucleic acids, proteins, and bacterial identification, integrable into small, portable devices. Recent work advances DNA nanopore design, self-assembled molecular sensors, and optical-tweezers control of DNA translocation. He also serves as Director of Graduate Education at the Cavendish Laboratory.

faculty.name: Eugene Terentjev
faculty.title: Professor of Polymer Physics
faculty.summary: Terentjev, Professor of Polymer Physics, studies the structure and dynamics of complex soft materials, including polymers, liquid crystals, and colloids, with growing impact on molecular and cell biophysics. He is a foundational figure in liquid crystal elastomers, co-authoring the standard monograph with the late Mark Warner. Recent work covers liquid-crystal elastomer actuators and sensors, mechanobiology of the cytoskeleton, protein folding, and self-assembly. His group couples theory with a purpose-built chemistry lab to advance stimuli-responsive and programmable materials.

faculty.name: Russell Cowburn
faculty.title: Professor of Physics
faculty.summary: Cowburn FRS returned to Cambridge in 2010 and researches nanoscale magnetism and spintronics, pioneering three-dimensional nanomagnetic systems. His group studies magnetic solitons and domain walls in multilayered synthetic antiferromagnets as data carriers for vertical, 3D data transfer, plus interconnected magnetic nanowire networks as candidate multistate memristors. Applications target low-energy computing, ultrahigh-density storage, and healthcare devices. A prolific inventor with many patents and start-ups, he bridges fundamental magnetization dynamics with commercial nanotechnology and anti-counterfeiting security.

faculty.name: Sandro Tacchella
faculty.title: Assistant Professor of Extragalactic Astrophysics
faculty.summary: Tacchella, Assistant Professor of Extragalactic Astrophysics and a member of the Kavli Institute for Cosmology, investigates how the first galaxies formed, how bulges and disks assemble, and how star formation shuts down in massive galaxies. He plays a key role in JWST NIRCam data processing and early-universe surveys. Recent 2025 work analyzing hundreds of low-mass galaxies shows early galaxies were turbulent and dynamically unsettled, growing through frequent mergers and bursts of star formation rather than smooth, orderly assembly.

faculty.name: Eloy de Lera Acedo
faculty.title: Professor of Radioastronomy
faculty.summary: De Lera Acedo, Professor of Radioastronomy, heads Cavendish Radio Astronomy and Cosmology, studying the infant Universe through the redshifted hyperfine 21-cm line from primordial hydrogen. He is international PI of the REACH experiment and the CosmoCube space mission, targeting the Dark Ages, Cosmic Dawn, and Epoch of Reionization. He leads Cambridge SKA development activities and sits on the HERA executive board. Recent work advances antenna design, foreground modeling, and receiver calibration needed to extract these extremely faint cosmological signals.

faculty.name: Tina Potter
faculty.title: Professor of High Energy Physics
faculty.summary: Potter, Professor of High Energy Physics, searches for physics beyond the Standard Model using the ATLAS detector at the LHC. Her research focuses on dark matter and supersymmetry, hunting for new particles produced in high-energy proton collisions and developing novel analysis techniques to isolate subtle signatures from overwhelming Standard Model backgrounds. She holds ATLAS experiment leadership responsibilities within the Cambridge group. Her work combines collider phenomenology, detector understanding, and statistical methods to constrain candidate explanations for dark matter.

faculty.name: Crispin Barnes
faculty.title: Professor of Quantum Physics
faculty.summary: Barnes, Professor of Quantum Physics, leads the Thin Film Magnetism and Quantum Information groups, with interests spanning quantum information theory, spintronics, materials science, and beyond. He operates bespoke molecular-beam-epitaxy, cleanroom, and low-temperature facilities to grow and measure magnetic oxides, topological insulators, and quantum devices. Recent work addresses fast, pulse-based state preparation in silicon spin qubits, deriving minimal evolution times for high-fidelity control. His eclectic program also touches environmental physics and financial modeling alongside solid-state quantum device engineering.

faculty.name: Anton Souslov
faculty.title: Associate Professor
faculty.summary: Souslov, Associate Professor in the Theory of Condensed Matter group, develops theories of soft and active materials, mechanical metamaterials, topological states, and polymer physics. He combines motors with elastic elements to describe self-driven, shape-changing matter, and uses topological band theory to design exotic classical waves, including the first optical fiber guiding light via a topological state. Recent work explores topological active matter, odd elasticity, and non-reciprocal mechanics, revealing robust edge modes and unusual responses in driven, out-of-equilibrium systems.

faculty.name: Didier Queloz
faculty.title: Jacksonian Professor of Natural Philosophy
faculty.summary: Queloz, Jacksonian Professor of Natural Philosophy and 2019 Nobel laureate for the first detection of an exoplanet around a Sun-like star, now leads efforts to detect Earth-like planets and assess their habitability. He directs the Leverhulme Centre for Life in the Universe, integrating astrophysics, chemistry, and biology to study the origins and prevalence of life. Recent work advances radial-velocity and transit instrumentation, atmospheric characterization of small planets, and interdisciplinary programs connecting exoplanet discovery to prebiotic chemistry and biosignatures.

funding.note: Doctoral researchers are employed with a salary (standard gross ~CHF 61,300 in year 1, rising annually) rather than paying tuition beyond a one-time ~CHF 1,500 fee.
